Lina — thanks for the clear summary. Recapping from Redwood's side + proposed next steps.

Recap / short answers:
- We can meet streaming p95 <=120ms for the expected payload distributions if we combine a modest warm pool + aggressive KV-prefix priming for active sessions.
- Sustained concurrency 800: achievable with reserved capacity + autoscale headroom.
- Burst to 2500 for ~10 min: achievable with warm-pool + fast-provision fallback, provided we accept a short tail (p99 degradation to ~300-350ms) during the steepest ramp.
- Scale-up target (80% capacity in 60s): our guidance is to keep a warm pool sized to cover the first 30-45% of the burst and rely on fractional-instance priming (warm GPU contexts) to cover the rest within 60s.

Proposed warm-pool strategy (initial recommendation):
- Maintain ~200 prewarmed contexts that keep KV caches warm for hot prefixes (priming approach).
- Fast path: prewarmed contexts handle immediate requests with <120ms p95.
- Slow path: autoscale backfills additional contexts; expect gradual p95 drift that recovers as new contexts finish priming (45–90s depending on model size and beam).
- Queueing behavior: soft queue with token-budgeting (we prioritize small/short requests during heavy tail); requests beyond soft limit are routed to a slimmer-model fallback to preserve throughput.

Next steps / owners (proposed):
- Redwood: deliver a detailed priming checklist and a short sim run showing predicted latency curve for your traffic distribution — owner: Vivek — ETA: 48 hours. (I attached the checklist + a sim summary.)
- FastFin: share the 24-hour traffic histogram and a canonical prompt set for priming — owner: Lina — ETA: 48 hours.
- Redwood infra (Karthik/Monica): sketch telemetry hooks we'll need in staging to validate warm-pool hit rate and p95 under surge — owner: Karthik — ETA: EOD Thu.
- Procurement: start drafting contract addendum for burst capacity (we'll provide SLO language) — owner: Tom — ETA: EOW.

Attachments: redwood-primer-checklist.pdf, sim-metrics-summary.csv

If that looks good I'll schedule a 30-min tech-run in your staging account to demo priming and observe the queueing behavior.

Cheers,
Vivek Kulkarni

Adding a few technical clarifications for the staging demo and telemetry so we're all aligned.

Priming overview (what we will do in staging):
- KV cache priming: we replay your canonical prompt set to warm KV layers per model shard. This reduces first-token latency for warmed contexts significantly.
- Fractional warm contexts: instead of full GPU instance spin-up, we keep a pool of preinitialized execution contexts (lighter-weight) to reduce cold-start time.
- Memory/throughput notes: for your model family (approx 70B fp16), each warm context consumes ~6–8 GB GPU memory; 200 contexts map to ~1.4TB of aggregate GPU memory footprint (shared across machines via colocated contexts).

Queueing behavior and SLO gating:
- Soft queue threshold: when warm-pool throughput saturates, we enforce a soft cap (configurable) on concurrent inflight requests queued for priming. Default suggestion: soft cap = 20% above prewarm capacity.
- Hard overflow: requests beyond soft cap are either throttled (retry-after header) or routed to a smaller quantized model. We'll demo both in staging so you can see p95/p99 tradeoffs.
- Observability hooks: token-latency histogram, warm-pool hit-rate, priming-completion time, and queue-depth timeline. We'll push a Grafana dashboard snapshot in the shared drive.

Sim notes (attached): our baseline sim (fast spike shape from your example profile) shows p95 stays <120ms until ~1600 concurrent sessions if warm-pool = 200. Beyond that p95 degrades but stays under 300ms for most of the 10-min window when we allow fallback routing. I'll include the CSV export with latency-by-concurrency numbers.

Let me know if FastFin wants us to bias warm-pool priming toward particular prompt prefixes — that improves hit rate for targeted flows.
